title: Citizenship Identity After State‐Led Resettlement: Institutional Inclusion, Place Attachment and Urban Membership
abstract: ABSTRACT Urbanization requires suburban farmers not only to relocate but also to reconstruct a sense of membership in urban society. This qualitative study develops an empirically grounded process model of citizenship identity among 22 resettled suburban farmers in Chengdu, China; the individual interviewee is the unit of analysis. Identity theory is the overarching lens. Institutional arrangements and everyday urban provision are interpreted through livelihood, security, belonging, esteem and future‐oriented needs; urban experience; and rural attachment. These meanings yield four context‐dependent citizenship‐identity positions: identification, suspicion, exclusion and a rural–urban identity dilemma. They are alternative outcomes, not fixed stages. Participants who described stronger citizenship identification also tended to describe more positive urban experiences and orientations. The study shows how rights, entitlements and local governance become identity‐relevant in state‐led resettlement.

journal.name: JOURNAL OF COMMUNITY & APPLIED SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY
